title: Rotate an Array Right by k
statement:
You get an array nums and a number k. Shift every element k places to the right. Elements that fall off the right end come back in at the left, in the same order.

Change nums in place; the function returns nothing. Note that k can be larger than the length of the array.

examples.why: The last two values wrap around to the front, keeping their order 23, 42.
Four shifts of a 3-element array is one full turn plus one shift, so only k mod 3 = 1 matters.
Shifting by exactly the length brings every element back to where it started.

hints: First reduce k: shifting by the length of the array changes nothing, so only k mod n matters.
With a second array it is easy: element i goes to index (i + k) mod n. Can you get there without the extra array?
Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the rest.

explain.intuition:
A right rotation by k takes the last k elements as one block and moves it in front of the first n − k elements. So the job is really "swap two blocks", and each block keeps its inner order.

Reversing the whole array puts the two blocks in the right places, but each block is now backwards. Reversing each block on its own turns it the right way round again. Three reversals, each done with two pointers walking toward each other, and no extra array.
steps: Set k = k mod n. If it is 0, stop.
Reverse the whole array: indexes 0 … n − 1.
Reverse the first block: indexes 0 … k − 1.
Reverse the second block: indexes k … n − 1.
pitfalls: Forgetting k mod n. With k > n the block boundaries fall outside the array.
Assigning a new array to the parameter (nums = [...]) instead of writing into it. The caller still holds the old array, so nothing changed.
Rotating left instead of right: reversing the blocks in the other order gives a left rotation by k.

solutions.title: Shift by one, k times
solutions.idea: Move the last element to the front, k mod n times. Correct, but each step moves the whole array.

solutions.title: Copy into place
solutions.idea: Element i belongs at (i + k) mod n. Write that into a copy, then copy it back.

solutions.title: Three reversals
solutions.idea: Reverse everything, then reverse each of the two blocks back. The blocks end up swapped with their inner order intact.

followups: Do it in O(1) extra space without reversals, by following cycles: each element jumps to (i + k) mod n. How many cycles are there? (Hint: gcd(n, k).)
How would you rotate a linked list by k instead?
